title: Non-overlapping Intervals
statement:
You're given a list of `intervals`, each written as `[start, end]`. Return the fewest intervals you have to remove so that none of the remaining intervals overlap.

Two intervals overlap when they share some stretch of the number line. Intervals that only touch at an endpoint, like `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]`, do not overlap. Only the number of removals is asked for, not which intervals to remove.

Constraints: 1 to 5,000 intervals; -50,000 <= start < end <= 50,000.

examples.explanation: The long interval [0, 5] overlaps all three others, so removing it leaves [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4].
Three identical intervals all overlap, so two must go.
Each interval only touches the next at an endpoint, which is allowed.

hints: Removing the fewest intervals is the same as keeping the most. What does a largest set of non-overlapping intervals look like on a number line?
Imagine choosing intervals one at a time. Which kind of interval leaves the most room for the ones that come later?
Test the rule 'always take the interval that starts earliest' on [1, 50], [2, 6], [5, 9], [8, 12]. Does it give the best answer? What other ordering could you use?
Once the intervals are sorted, you only need to remember where the last kept interval ended. When is the next interval compatible, and what if the endpoints are equal?
Sort by end time and keep the first interval. For each next one: if its start is at least the last kept end, keep it and update the end; otherwise count one removal.
followUps: Can you explain why picking the earliest-finishing interval is always safe?
What are the time and space complexity, and where does the time go?
What would change if intervals that only touch, like [1, 2] and [2, 3], counted as overlapping?
What if every interval had a weight and you wanted to keep the maximum total weight instead?
idealAnswerPoints: Reframes the task as keeping the maximum number of compatible intervals
Sorts by end time and greedily keeps each interval that starts at or after the last kept end
Counts a removal whenever an interval overlaps the last kept one
Treats touching endpoints as compatible (>=, not >)
Gives the exchange argument for why the earliest end is safe, and states O(n log n) time
weakAnswerSigns: Sorts by start time and takes the first interval, which keeps a long interval that blocks many short ones
Tries every subset of intervals or a recursion with no memoization
Treats touching intervals as overlapping and over-counts the removals
Cannot explain why the greedy choice is correct

rubric.correctness: Matches the minimum removals for nested, identical, touching, negative-range and large inputs.
rubric.efficiency: O(n log n) with a sort by end and one pass; exponential or quadratic search is below the bar.
rubric.code_quality: Sort key stated plainly, one running last_end variable, a single clear compatibility check.
rubric.communication: Counterexamples the sort-by-start idea and justifies the greedy choice before coding.
